ai_comments:
YTA

You agreed to attend this party and participated in the planning, even reluctantly. While your SIL's actions in sticking you with the tab are incredibly rude and presumptuous, your husband is the primary person who should have handled this situation. The financial responsibility for his own birthday party should have been discussed and clarified with his sister beforehand, and this is a failure in communication between the two of them. Your anger is misdirected; you should be holding your husband accountable for not managing his family and the expectations for his event. Being cold to your SIL and complaining to your kids doesn't address the core issue.

YTA

The sister-in-law suggested the party, but she never offered to foot the bill. You and your husband chose to attend and spend the money, and the costs were yours to negotiate up front. Your frustration is understandable, but assuming she would pay and then treating her coldly and blaming her after the fact for a cost you never clarified makes you the asshole here.

YTA

The user's sister-in-law suggested the party, but the husband agreed to it, and the user also agreed to attend, saying "if you want it, I will go." The user knew beforehand they wouldn't enjoy the party but still chose to go, serving as designated driver and mingling with the guests. While being stuck with the tab is upsetting, it's unclear whether the sister-in-law explicitly agreed to pay. The user didn't clarify the costs beforehand. Being cold and angry towards the sister-in-law seems unreasonable; they could have handled this more constructively by discussing the financial arrangements with their husband or sister-in-law before the party.

NTA

Your sister-in-law's suggestion to throw your husband a party turned into a massive, expensive event that you never agreed to organize or fund. Being stuck with a nearly $2,000 tab-on top of thousands in other costs-with no prior discussion is completely unreasonable. You supported your husband by attending despite your discomfort, but being suddenly made responsible for the financial burden she created crosses a major line. Your frustration is completely valid, and you're not the asshole for being angry over this situation.

NTA

You were not responsible for organizing or funding the event, and your sister-in-law overstepped by placing the financial burden on you without prior discussion. You supported your husband by attending despite discomfort, serving as designated driver and managing logistics. Being upset about the unexpected $2,000 bar tab and nearly $3,000 total cost for a party she proposed and orchestrated, which you didn't want or enjoy, is completely reasonable. Holding her accountable and setting boundaries doesn't make you the asshole.

NTA

Your boyfriend prioritized his own comfort and jealousy over a milestone event that was important to you. His excuse that he would have come if there were only three people is irrelevant, as that was not the case for your party. The fact that he then attended his friend's party, even after initially claiming he wouldn't, demonstrates a clear double standard and a lack of consideration for your feelings. While his point about feeling uncomfortable is valid, a supportive partner would make an effort for a significant occasion, especially when you explicitly asked him to be there. His actions show a lack of prioritization for your relationship.

NTA

Your boyfriend skipped your birthday out of jealousy and discomfort, yet attended another friend's party after saying he wouldn't. That double standard disregards an event important to you. Your frustration is reasonable, especially when you'd still attend his birthday despite discomfort, and you're not the asshole.

YTA

Your boyfriend's decision not to attend your birthday party because he was uncomfortable around your friends, especially one he's jealous of, is understandable to some extent. However, your anger towards him for attending his friend's birthday party afterwards is also valid. Nevertheless, your expectation that he should prioritize your feelings and birthday over his own discomfort, and your comparison to how you would act in a similar situation, overlooks the fact that people have different boundaries and comfort levels in social situations. Furthermore, his willingness to attend his friend's party due to exceptional circumstances (the belief that there would only be three people) doesn't necessarily negate his initial decision regarding your party. Your demand for understanding while not fully reciprocating it places you in a position where you're not entirely open to his point of view, hence making you the asshole in this scenario.

YTA

Your boyfriend's reasoning is consistent, even if it stings. He didn't skip your birthday because he doesn't care; he skipped because of his discomfort around a specific friend. When his friend's GF tapped him to save her party, he had a clear, time-sensitive reason to go-one that didn't involve facing the same jealousy issue. Comparing your own efforts (like your socially anxious friend attending) ignores that he flagged his boundaries upfront and even offered you the same freedom for his birthday. Relationships should prioritize mutual understanding, not scoreboard logic. You're hurt, but his actions don't make him an asshole.

NTA

Your birthday was important to you, especially as a milestone moment after feeling isolated growing up. You asked your boyfriend to attend, and he refused-not due to a scheduling conflict or prior commitment, but because of unfounded jealousy toward a friend he's never even met. That's a personal choice rooted in insecurity, not a valid excuse. Meanwhile, he ended up attending his friend's birthday, even going so far as to bring three extra people to "help" with guest numbers, which contradicts his claim that he wouldn't attend your event for similar reasons. His argument that you wouldn't be obligated to attend his birthday if you felt uncomfortable doesn't hold weight-this is about reciprocity and respect in a relationship, especially when you've extended that support in return. While it's understandable he might feel uneasy, his refusal to support you on such an important day-while showing up for others-justifies your hurt and anger.

NTA

His arbitrary "driver picks the music" rule and insistence on a formal agreement are controlling and dismissive, despite the favor he's doing you. A healthy partnership requires mutual respect and compromise. You've apologized for the past mistake and communicated your desire to share music with him. Refusing to trust your word and insisting on musical dominance for most of the trip makes his help feel transactional rather than supportive.

NTA

The request to sign a "contract" giving him control of most of an 8-hour drive's music is unreasonable and overly controlling, especially given the huge favor of traveling that far to help you move. Music is a minor, negotiable detail, and wanting a balanced share or mixed tastes is reasonable. Insisting on written control makes the help feel conditional and diminishes your enjoyment. You've apologized for the past misunderstanding and tried to communicate your perspective; his demand is the problem.

NTA

His overly controlling reaction and insecurity about music are understandable given the past incident, but his "contract" comes across as petty and conditional. You've reassured him that you're willing to compromise and listen to his music, so expecting trust and respect in return is reasonable. Although you appreciate his help with the move, you're not unreasonable to feel that his help is being offered conditionally and your enjoyment and preferences are being dismissed.

NTA

Turning a music preference into a legally styled contract is a massive overreaction that infantilizes you both. While his help with the move is appreciated, it doesn't grant him control over the whole trip, especially something as trivial as music. Road trips are about shared experiences, and compromise is a natural part of that. Enforcing rigid rules instead of trusting you after your previous conversation makes this about control, respect and communication. Your feelings of being unappreciated are valid.

NTA

You're not the asshole for feeling hurt and disrespected by being asked to sign a "contract" over music rights during a road trip. While your boyfriend may be trying to prevent conflict based on a past incident, turning a minor issue into a formal agreement comes across as controlling and unnecessarily rigid. Compromise is reasonable-like splitting listening time or creating a shared playlist-but demanding a signed contract crosses a line into treating a relationship like a transaction. His actions suggest he values being "right" or "in control" over mutual trust and flexibility. You've already apologized for the previous incident and expressed your desire to share music as a bonding experience, which shows emotional maturity. His refusal to trust your word and insistence on a contract makes this about power, not fairness. That said, his effort to help you move is commendable, but it doesn't justify making you feel invalidated. A healthy compromise doesn't require paperwork.

YTA

Dave is breaking your agreed no-shoes rule. However, rather than communicate or compromise, you deliberately retaliated, using his own words against him. While you enjoy those foods, your primary motivation was to annoy him. Two wrongs don't make a right; this passive-aggressive behavior escalates the conflict instead of resolving it.

ESH

Both of you are in the wrong. Dave broke the original agreement about shoes and should have respected the compromise you discussed. In response, you escalated the conflict by deliberately cooking strong-smelling foods to annoy him, which is a petty retaliation rather than a reasonable solution. Neither behavior is justified, and both of you need to communicate more constructively and respect each other's boundaries.

YTA

You and your roommate initially agreed on no shoes inside, and he has disregarded that rule. However, instead of addressing it constructively by reminding him of the agreement or finding a compromise, you deliberately cooked strong-smelling foods that you knew he disliked. Trying to annoy him was equally disrespectful and petty. You escalated the situation and created more tension, rather than resolving the issue or finding a mutually respectful solution.

ESH

You both agreed to no shoes indoors; Dave is an asshole for breaking that rule and disrespecting the shared space and your attempts to resolve it. Intentionally cooking pungent foods to "get back at him" is childish and creates a hostile shared environment. You're an asshole as well. Both of you prioritize personal comfort over mutual respect and compromise, escalating rather than solving the conflict.

YTA

You agreed to a mutual living arrangement and, when your roommate broke one rule (no shoes indoors), you responded by intentionally violating another unspoken expectation (not deliberately cooking strong-smelling foods to retaliate). While his disregard for the shoe rule is disrespectful, your actions weren't about maintaining household harmony-they were about getting back at him. Deliberately cooking pungent foods knowing it would upset him, especially as a form of payback, escalates conflict rather than resolving it. Mature cohabitation requires communication and compromise, not petty retaliation. You're both at fault, but your intentional provocation makes you the bigger asshole here.

NTA

Your request is based on a legitimate and scientifically-backed hygiene concern, as flushing with the lid up does aerosolize bacteria and waste particles. Your partner initially agreed to this boundary and then reneged, dismissing your valid feelings when you hold him to his word. His annoyance at being reminded, after he explicitly asked for reminders, makes him the asshole in this situation. It is a minor habit change for a significant gain in shared household cleanliness and respect for your peace of mind.

NTA

The request to put the toilet lid down before flushing is a reasonable hygiene concern, especially given the fear of aerosolized particles landing on surfaces like toothbrushes. Your partner agreed to the habit and even invited reminders, which makes reminding him appropriate rather than abusive. His annoyance stems more from inconvenience than from any real wrongdoing, and his dismissal of a legitimate health-related request is inconsiderate. Since you're simply trying to keep your shared space clean and have asked for a simple habit change that he initially accepted, you're not the asshole for insisting on it.

NTA

Your cleanliness concern is valid, and your partner agreed to put the lid down before flushing. Reminding him when he forgets is reasonable, especially since he asked you to. His inconsistency and dismissiveness are frustrating; expecting him to honor his agreement is fair in a shared space where cleanliness affects both of you.

NTA

Your request to put the toilet lid down before flushing is reasonable and based on factual concerns about hygiene. Your boyfriend agreed to the rule and even encouraged you to remind him, so his annoyance when you follow through seems inconsistent and dismissive. While changing habits can be difficult, the issue isn't the size of the ask-it's his failure to honor his agreement and respect your feelings in a shared home. Communication and compromise are key, but you're not wrong for insisting on a simple, agreed-upon measure that matters to you.

NTA

Wanting the toilet lid down before flushing is a hygiene concern you've communicated clearly. Your partner agreed, then resented reminders, which is inconsistent and dismissive; those mixed signals create the conflict, not your request. Expecting follow-through on agreed-upon habits is reasonable, particularly when they affect your comfort and sense of cleanliness in a shared home.

NTA

A 17-year-old is old enough to take responsibility for an appliance they turned on; falling asleep while it preheats is negligent. Your anger reflects a parent's responsibility for safety and preparation for independent living. While their initial expectation to be notified might have been reasonable, failing to follow through and shifting blame onto you is not. Your reaction was justified.

NTA

The teen was responsible for the oven they turned on. Leaving a hot oven on while falling asleep is unsafe and shows a lack of basic responsibility, especially for someone living independently soon. Even if the parent's reminder was a bit delayed, the teen should have checked the oven themselves rather than assuming they'd be notified. The parent's frustration, while perhaps a bit loud, wasn't unreasonable given the potential fire hazard.

NTA

The child's decision to sleep with the oven on was reckless and risked fire or accidents. Expecting someone else to monitor the oven and notify them when it was ready was unreasonable. The OP's anger, although possibly excessive, reflected legitimate concerns about safety, responsibility and independent living. Wanting to teach responsibility and self-care makes their reaction not entirely unjustified.

NTA

A 17-year-old is nearly an adult and should understand basic safety, especially when operating a potentially dangerous appliance like an oven. Leaving a 450-degree oven unattended to take a nap is a serious fire hazard, regardless of whether they thought you would alert them. Your anger wasn't about them falling asleep; it was about the dangerous lack of responsibility. Your kid needs to learn that safety is their own responsibility, not someone else's. You're not overreacting; you're parenting to ensure they don't harm themselves or others when they're on their own.

NTA

At 17, your child is nearing adulthood and should be expected to handle basic responsibilities like cooking safely. Leaving an oven on at 450 degrees F while falling asleep is a serious fire hazard and could have led to catastrophic consequences. Your frustration is valid, especially since you already alerted them that the oven was preheated. Expecting you to monitor it and wake them undermines accountability. Your anger reflects legitimate safety concerns and preparation for independent living, not overreaction.

NTA

Alice eats a larger share and insists on toppings only she prefers. Asking her to pay for her own pizza lets you and Connor enjoy your toppings and enough food. Her money constraints are unfortunate, but don't outweigh fairness, especially when the price difference is minimal.

YTA

The OP's insistence on preferred toppings ignores others' needs or constraints, especially Alice's large appetite and limited money. The split forces her to pay extra for a medium she'll likely eat all by herself or accept a larger share of a pizza she won't enjoy. That selfish compromise dismisses the group's decision and unfairly burdens her. A larger pizza with mixed toppings or a half-and-half would be a more reasonable middle ground.

NTA

Asking Alice to get her own pizza is reasonable given her large appetite and picky eating. The small price difference isn't asking her to break the bank. By doubling down on your suggestion, you're advocating for the toppings you and Connor want. Her reluctance may reflect not wanting to pay more, but the request is fair.

NTA

This is about toppings and portions, not her eating more. Alice wants pepperoni, you chicken and veggie, and Connor vegetarian. Suggesting her own medium rather than insisting she pay more for a shared pizza is accommodating and a reasonable compromise. Everyone gets what they want, the price difference is minimal, and you and Connor aren't subsidizing pizza you dislike.

NTA

Alice eats significantly more, and her specific preferences limit everyone's options; she'd eat nearly half the food if it were split three ways. Separate pizzas let everyone enjoy their toppings, and paying slightly more for eating more is fair. She may be sensitive about money, but the minimal difference isn't burdensome. You're advocating fairness, not being hostile or malicious.

NTA

Your husband has repeatedly prioritized his softball league and friends over your relationship, from cutting your honeymoon short to ignoring your valid concerns about his health. You're not obligated to spend free time feeling uncomfortable, unsupported and lonely. Supporting his hobby doesn't require attending every game, especially with teammates who are poor influences and disrespect your relationship. Framing your reasonable boundary as making him "choose" is unfair.

NTA

Your husband's hobby doesn't obligate you to attend, especially after he already sacrificed part of your honeymoon for it. Teammates encouraged delaying elbow surgery, and the manager spread false gossip, making games uncomfortable and potentially harmful to his health. You communicated your feelings and let him play without you; you didn't force him to quit. Expecting support in that toxic setting doesn't make your refusal wrong.

NTA

Wanting to cut your honeymoon short and potentially worsening his elbow for softball sometimes put the sport above your feelings. His teammates' gossip and poor advice justify your discomfort around them. You're limiting attendance, not stopping him playing; protecting your emotional well-being doesn't mean withholding support.

NTA

Your husband has consistently prioritized this "recreational" softball league over significant moments in your marriage and even his own health. The honeymoon incident alone was a massive red flag - demanding to cut your honeymoon short for a casual sports game shows a serious lack of priority-setting. His friends on the team have demonstrated they don't have his best interests at heart, with one actively encouraging him to postpone necessary medical treatment. You're not asking him to stop playing; you're simply setting a reasonable boundary to protect your own emotional well-being by choosing not to watch him with people who don't respect him (or your marriage) and make you feel lonely. Truly supporting your husband isn't about blindly attending every game - it's about caring for someone's overall wellbeing, which includes their marriage and health. You're not making him choose "softball or nothing" - you're choosing yourself when he consistently fails to do so.

NTA

Your husband repeatedly put softball above shared experiences, including asking to cut your honeymoon short-something deeply meaningful and once-in-a-lifetime. His friends encouraged delaying medical care and spread harmful gossip. You're reasonably protecting your emotional well-being by declining to attend, while making clear he can continue playing. Supporting him doesn't require enduring emotional distress or toxic company.

NTA

You made a reasonable proposal for a shared house that would benefit everyone, particularly given your son's severe allergy. They chose the cheaper hotel option, which is their right, but that choice came with the consequence of not having a kitchen. It is not greedy to expect them to contribute to the cost of the amenity they now want to use, especially since you are bearing the entire financial burden for it. They are the ones trying to get the benefit without sharing the cost.

NTA

The other families chose to stay in hotels and explicitly opted out of the house rental. You paid extra to secure a place with a kitchen for legitimate reasons (allergy concerns, convenience). It's reasonable to expect them to either stay in their hotels or contribute to the cost if they want to use the kitchen you're paying for. Refusing free use of the kitchen isn't greedy.

NTA

You proposed a house rental that would benefit everyone. Everyone initially agreed, but the others backed out over cost. You and your wife still rented for your family's needs, including your son's food allergy. Wanting the kitchen without contributing isn't fair. Asking them to cover the extra $50/night is reasonable when you're shouldering that additional expense.

NTA

Your son's severe nut allergy made a kitchen a necessity, not a luxury. The family declined your shared rental for cheaper hotels, then expected its main benefit free. Like declining a timeshare but wanting its facilities, that ignores who paid. Asking them to contribute is a fair consequence and a reasonable boundary, not greed.

NTA

You proposed shared accommodations that benefited everyone, especially your child with a severe allergy. By choosing cheaper hotels, the family opted out of paying for a kitchen. Expecting a contribution now is fair. You're not obligated to share your privately funded rental for free, particularly if that increases costs or reduces your family's privacy and comfort. That's fairness, not greed.

YTA

You deliberately sabotaged your classmates' academic performance by feeding them false information to artificially lower the class average, enabling you to benefit from a curve. While their cheating is wrong, your actions were premeditated and harmed others solely for your personal gain. This is a severe breach of academic integrity and basic decency.

YTA

Your scheme was deliberately designed to damage your classmates' academic performance so that you could benefit from it. You provided them with false information intended to make them fail, manipulating both your classmates and the teacher. That deliberate sabotage is unethical and dishonest, making you the clear asshole in this situation.

YTA

You deliberately misled your classmates to fail a test, taking advantage of their reliance on your hour's information to study, and then manipulated the situation to benefit yourself by getting the teacher to curve the test. These actions were premeditated and intended to harm others' grades while improving your own, which is unfair and dishonest. Your classmates' past cheating doesn't excuse your own wrongdoing or give you the right to sabotage their grades. Your actions were selfish and caused harm to others, making you the asshole in this situation.

YTA

You purposefully and systematically sabotaged your classmates' academic careers by creating a coordinated disinformation campaign. While their cheating was also wrong, two wrongs don't make a right. You also followed this up by exploiting your good relationship with the teacher for personal gain, framing the low scores (that you engineered) as a problem with online learning rather than a result of your own scheme. Your actions were calculated, malicious, and went far beyond simply not helping them cheat.

YTA

You deliberately misled classmates to manipulate the grading curve for your own benefit. Your classmates were wrong to cheat by relying on others for test information, but exploiting that system instead of disengaging, studying harder or seeking legitimate help was selfish and dishonest. You sabotaged their academic performance, then compounded the deception by collectively lobbying the teacher with a misleading claim about online learning impacting performance. Your actions were premeditated and harmful, making you the asshole.
